blocks.text: Because of the wonderful endowments we have noted in the eagle, whatever is lofty in heaven or most excellent on earth (God, that is, the angels, the faithful, empires and the greatest kings) is compared with the eagle by the sacred writers. Thus God says to the Israelites, whom he had led out of Egypt, Exod. XIX, 4. You have seen what I have done to the Egyptians, and how I bore you up on eagles' wings, i.e. ὡσεὶ ἐπὶ πτερύγων ἀετοῦ [hōsei epi pterygōn aetou], as upon eagles' wings, as the Greeks rightly render it, and the three Chaldees, and the Syriac, and one of the Arabic versions, adding the mark of comparison, which must necessarily be supplied in this place. Yet the divine writer did not suppress it without reason. That is, so that the comparison might be more vivid and strike the mind more, he attributes to God eagle's wings, with which he carried the Israelites from Egypt into Arabia. So that we may know that he behaved toward his people in the same way as the eagle usually does toward its brood. For Scripture is accustomed to give the thing signified the name of the sign, and in turn to give the sign the name of the thing signified. Further, the reason for the figure is explained in various ways. Some refer it to the eagle's swiftness, because God had led so many myriads of people out of Egypt in a single day. Others to the ease of its flight, because this was done without any effort, and Israel had escaped from so monstrous a servitude as easily as the eagle flies. Others to the eagle's lofty flight, by which it carries both itself and its chicks beyond all range of missiles. For so God had preserved his own with a mighty hand, and had set them, as it were, on high, so that the weapons of the enemy might not reach them. Jonathan paraphrases (παραφράζει [paraphrazei]) the words of the sacred text thus: טעית יתכון על עננין היך על גדפי נשרין מן פילוסין, I carried you upon clouds, as upon eagles' wings, from the city of Pelusium. Not much differently the Jerusalem translator. That is, they invent for themselves this miracle, about which Scripture is entirely silent: that God carried the Israelites upon clouds from the region of Pelusium all the way to Mount Sinai. Nor are there lacking those who observe that of two chicks the eagle feeds and rears only one, casting out the other, so as to refer this to God, who loved Jacob and hated Esau, content to choose one of two peoples [II, 767] and acknowledge it as his own. But no one is a better interpreter of the words of Moses than Moses himself, in these words of his Song, Deut. XXXII, 11. As an eagle stirs up its nest [col. 183] and hovers over its young with outspread wings, and takes them and carries them on its pinions, so the Lord alone led him, etc. He made him ride on the heights of the earth etc. Since what is said there of the eagle has already been explained, it remains for us to show how these things apply to God. Nor is the matter obscure. The eagle rouses with its cry the chicks lying sluggish in the filth of the nest, to provoke them to flight. So God, by his word, stirred up the Israelites, so oppressed by wretched servitude that they did not aspire to liberation, to obey the champions of liberty raised up for them by God. The eagle hovers over its chicks with outspread wings. So the Spirit moves over those in whom he works effectually. For Moses uses the same word when he says at the creation that the Spirit of God moved upon the waters. And that power of the divine Spirit bent the Israelites, otherwise intractable, to obedience. Moreover, he spread over them the wings of his providence, of which Scripture speaks so often. As when in Ruth. II, 12. she is said to have come under the wings of God to shelter herself. And when the godly are said to be hidden, to take refuge, to sing, and to be protected under the shadow or in the covert of his wings, Psal. XVII, 8. and XXXVI, 8. and LVII, 2. and LXI, 5. and LXIII, 8. and XCI, 4. etc. This was signified by the cloud that covered the Israelites, Num. XIV, 14. Finally, with the same wings he carried them on this journey, as the eagle carries its chicks, whenever he kept them from falling or from stumbling on a slippery and rough road exposed to many dangers. Accordingly you read elsewhere that God carried them in his arms, like παῖδας ὑπαγκαλίους [paidas hypankalious]. Thus Deut. I, 31. The Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his little son, all the way that you went until you came to this place. And Os. XI, 1. 3. When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son, etc. Where the Chaldee paraphrase has: And I, through an angel sent from my presence, led Israel by a fitting way: ונטלתנון כר על דרעין, and I carried them as upon arms. Indeed, it is said to the godly man in Psal. XCI, 11. He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone. It should be noted that, as in the Law, so also in the Gospel the church is compared to chicks which the mother warms and protects under her wings. But in the Law that mother is an eagle, and in the Gospel a hen; and thus, as they would have it, the different dispensation under each Testament is foreshadowed. The one of power, which God displayed when he led his people out of Egypt with a strong right hand and an outstretched arm and brought them into the promised land. The other of grace, when Christ came lowly, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself even to the death of the cross. Yet in such a way that in both God's supreme love shines forth, and the care he takes of his own. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that in the New Testament too God sometimes delivers his own with power. Accordingly, as the Jewish church, when on the point of being crushed by Pharaoh, was borne up on eagles' wings and carried into the desert, so [II, 768] in Apoc. XXII, 14. the Christian church too is given two great wings, with which to fly into the desert from the sight of the dragon. Of him Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was a figure, who himself is also called a dragon in Ezech. XXIX, 3.
